chunks: Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated from Ibn Muskān, from al-Ḥasan al-Ṣayqal, who said:

I was sitting with Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) when he sent one of his non-Arab servant boys on an errand to a person. The boy left and then returned, so Abū ʿAbdillāh began asking him for the answer/explanation, but the young lad did not understand him, and this happened a number of times. He (the narrator) said: When I saw that his speech did not change and he was not able to understand, I thought that Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) would get angry on him. He said: Abū ʿAbdillāh (peace be upon him) looked at him sternly and then said: 'By Allah, even if you are unable to speak with your tongue, you are not unable to communicate with your heart [and mind].' Then he said: 'Verily modesty, chastity, and inarticulateness – the inarticulateness of the tongue, not of the heart – are part of faith, while immodesty, obscenity and insolence are part of hypocrisy.'
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between inarticulateness of the tongue and inarticulateness of the heart in Shia ethics?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Kitab al-Zuhd*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between linguistic inarticulateness (*al-‘ayy*) and spiritual deficiency, clarifying that a non-Arab servant’s struggle with language is not a defect of the heart. He establishes *al-‘ayy* (modesty in speech) as a core component of faith (*Iman*), contrasting it with *al-fahsh* (immodesty) and *al-salata* (insolence), which are markers of hypocrisy (*Nifaq*). This highlights the Shia emphasis on internal sincerity over external eloquence or ethnic background.
